source.title: The Curious Case of Convex Neural Networks
source.authors: S. Sivaprasad; Ankur Singh; Naresh Manwani; Vineet Gandhi

page_placements.theme: Modified training can suppress or reverse corrupted-target fitting

record.tranche_reason: The study tests random and partially randomized labels, finding that its constrained IOC networks resist fitting noise while the standard AllConv baseline memorizes it at convergence.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2016) and Arpit et al. (2017) for prior results; those cited results are not extracted as rows. Rows below cover this study’s own randomized-label experiments. Table 3 reports AllConv and IOC-AllConv across five noise levels at peak and convergence. The table’s flattened layout permits the values to be assigned to the model and noise conditions.
record.test_reason: The study repeats random-label and partial-label-corruption experiments, measuring training and test accuracy in standard MLP and AllConv networks. These results bear on V1, V4 and V6. Its constrained IOC models demonstrate a mitigation, rather than refuting claims about standard networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the random-label experiments: the authors conclude that IOC constraints resist noisy-label fitting, whereas standard networks first learn a simpler hypothesis and later memorize noise. Their broader conclusion also claims improved generalization and calibration while retaining useful classification capacity.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses randomized and partially randomized training labels on image-classification networks, comparing AllConv with an IOC-constrained counterpart. The IOC model changes the activation and imposes weight constraints; training and augmentation strategies are described as the same for comparative studies. The paper cites the original random-label experiment but does not claim to replicate its full settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise fraction changes the reported train and test accuracies; results are reported at peak and convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: IOC-AllConv resists fitting noisy labels: at full corruption its convergence training accuracy is 10.21%, and at partial corruption it retains substantially higher test accuracy than standard AllConv.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Imposing input-output convexity through weight constraints and activation choices can suppress random-label memorization while retaining useful learning from remaining signal.

record.problems: The random-label evidence is shown for MLP in a figure description and for AllConv in a single dataset sweep. Results are reported at peak and convergence but no training-time comparison or exact hyperparameter match to the original study is given. The convergence train accuracy at 100% noise is 97.80%, not zero training error.

untested.parts: The text does not explicitly verify that architecture and training hyperparameters remain identical between true-label and fully random-label runs.
No measured training-time ratio or comparison of convergence speed across corruption fractions. The constant-factor statement is cited prior work.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
Only a discrete corruption sweep is reported; the experiment does not establish behavior at every intermediate fraction.
No weight-decay, dropout or augmentation ablation tests random-label fitting or generalization after removing those regularizers. IOC functional constraints are a different intervention.
No quantitative separation of clean-label and noisy-label learning times or direct comparison of fully real-label and fully random-label learning dynamics.

missing.what: Standard AllConv peak-checkpoint train/test accuracies at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% corruption: 72.8/85.72, 56.48/80.47, 38.52/75.80 and 22.40/60.24. Compared with convergence, these show training fit increasing while test performance deteriorates, providing quantitative evidence relevant to the reported learning sequence.
missing.locator: Table 3; Results, Robustness to random label noise

missing.what: The clean-label AllConv reference reports 99.31% training and 92.8% test accuracy. It supplies the zero-corruption endpoint absent from the extracted noise sweep, although Table 2 is a separate reported experiment.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3's extracted numerical assignments are correct. Near-zero training error is permitted by V1, so 97.80% accuracy alone does not warrant a V1 limits_scope verdict. V4 explicitly requires perfect training fit, making the residual training errors a qualification. IOC results do not justify extending that qualification to standard networks.

versions.untested_parts: The reported standard-network random-label results are for MLP in the CIFAR-10 figure and AllConv in the CIFAR-10 noise sweep; other architectures, datasets and training hyperparameters are not tested with fully random labels.

Only AllConv and its IOC counterpart are tested, on CIFAR-10 at 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% randomized training labels; this is not a continuous sweep. The study reports test accuracy rather than test error.
The study reports the qualitative learning sequence for AllConv and IOC-AllConv with 50% noisy labels; it does not quantify when patterns or noise are learned.

rows.subject: AllConv
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with randomized training labels; convergence results reported.
rows.note: At full label randomization the convergence train accuracy is near 100% and test accuracy is near chance; Table 3 also reports peak results in R3.
rows.check: The values are correct. Training accuracy of 97.80% meets V1's near-zero-error allowance but incompletely meets V4's perfect-fitting requirement; the shared state reflects that distinction. Convergence means loss below 0.001 or reaching 2000 epochs.
